evals.prompt: I'm building an invoicing feature. Right now each operation is a short script — create invoice, mark paid, void. A teammate says we should build a proper Domain Model with entities and aggregates from the start. Should we?
evals.expected_output: Agent chooses the business-logic pattern by force and does not escalate to a Domain Model without evidence.
expectations: Agent says a Transaction Script is fine while the logic stays short and independent
Agent names the escalation trigger — duplicated decisions/validation, or real invariants and lifecycle appearing — as what would justify moving to a Domain Model
Agent does NOT recommend a full Domain Model / aggregates just because it is 'proper'
If it does discuss rich domain modeling, it defers that to domain-driven-design rather than owning it here

evals.prompt: Two support agents open the same customer record, both edit it over a few minutes in their browsers, and whoever saves last silently wipes the other's changes. How should I prevent this?
evals.expected_output: Agent recognizes an offline (cross-request) concurrency problem and recommends an offline lock, distinct from DB isolation.
expectations: Agent identifies this as a business transaction spanning a user think-time gap, not something a database transaction/lock covers
Agent recommends an Optimistic Offline Lock (version/timestamp checked on save) as the default, surfacing conflict resolution to the user
Agent mentions Pessimistic Offline Lock as the alternative only when contention is high enough to justify blocking
Agent does NOT answer with database isolation levels as the primary fix (that would be data-intensive's ground)

evals.prompt: We're moving to a horizontally scaled, stateless web tier behind a load balancer. Where should we keep per-user session state?
evals.expected_output: Agent weighs client/server/database session placement by its forces rather than picking one by default.
expectations: Agent lays out client vs server vs database session state as a deliberate choice
Agent ties the choice to the stated forces — statelessness/scaling favors client or database over in-memory server state
Agent names the risks of the client option (integrity/security) and the database option (extra load, stale-row cleanup)
Agent insists the session have a clear owner, lifetime, and cleanup story

evals.prompt: Our repository layer is one generic class with save(), get(), list(), delete() over every table, and the controllers call SQL-ish query helpers directly and also open transactions. Is this a good structure?
evals.expected_output: Agent flags the generic-repository and controller-centric anti-patterns as review blockers and reshapes responsibilities.
expectations: Agent flags the generic CRUD repository shaped by tables (not use cases) as a forbidden pattern to reshape
Agent flags the controller owning transactions/SQL/workflow and moves coordination into an application/service operation with explicit transaction ownership
Agent recommends repositories shaped by what the application actually asks for
Agent does NOT endorse the current structure as fine

evals.prompt: I want to split my order module out into a separate microservice so it's cleaner. The web layer would make a remote call for each order line to build the page. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Agent pushes back on distributing by default and, if remote, insists on a coarse boundary.
expectations: Agent applies don't-distribute-by-default — keep it in-process unless a real boundary forces the split
Agent identifies the per-order-line remote call as a chatty interface / distributed-object smell
Agent recommends a coarse-grained Remote Facade with DTOs (one batched round-trip) if the split is truly needed
Agent notes the latency/serialization/partial-failure cost being taken on, cross-linking production-readiness rather than restating retry/timeout mechanics

evals.prompt: Within one save operation I load the same product twice through different relationships and end up with two in-memory Product objects that drift out of sync, and I'm not sure when each gets written to the DB. Help.
evals.expected_output: Agent reaches for Identity Map and Unit of Work to make identity scope and write timing explicit.
expectations: Agent names Identity Map — one in-memory instance per identity per scope — as the fix for the duplicate objects
Agent names Unit of Work to make the write coordination one logical, explicitly-owned commit
Agent calls out making loading behavior visible to avoid hidden auto-persistence / N+1 surprises
Agent keeps the transaction boundary short and explicit rather than scattering saves across callers
